re_line: Xi's Washington visit, $30 billion tariff swap, Taiwan arms package on hold, Second Thomas Shoal standoff, Senate punts Chinese car ban
editors_note: This is the first China Room Brief. It arrives every Friday with the week in U.S.-China relations and what CSIS scholars have coming.

week_at_a_glance.headline: China's Golden Week holiday ends
week_at_a_glance.body: China's seven-day National Day holiday concludes on October 7. Traders are watching whether Beijing resumes approvals for refiners' fuel exports. Reuters reported those exports were suspended for October beyond Hong Kong and Macau, and PetroChina cancelled some gasoline and jet-fuel cargoes on September 30.

week_at_a_glance.headline: PBOC runs 1.2 trillion yuan reverse repo
week_at_a_glance.body: A 1.2 trillion yuan three-month buyout reverse repo operation is set for October 8, part of a package Reuters reported alongside a nationwide mortgage-interest subsidy and a cut to the Pledged Supplementary Lending rate. Analysts told Bloomberg the "mini stimulus" will likely secure the year's GDP target but deliver little additional lift.

week_at_a_glance.headline: IMF and World Bank meet in Bangkok
week_at_a_glance.body: The IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings run October 12 to 18 in Bangkok, Thailand, where China's growth trajectory and debt-related concerns typically feature prominently. China's official manufacturing PMI returned to expansion at 50.1 in September, CNBC reported.

week_at_a_glance.headline: Bloomberg New Economy Forum opens in New Delhi
week_at_a_glance.body: Watch for an explicit "levers of power" framing amid U.S.-China-India triangulation at the October 13 to 15 forum.

heard_on_the_hill.headline: Senate puts off permanent Chinese car ban
heard_on_the_hill.body: The Senate punted a bill to permanently ban Chinese-made cars from the U.S. market until after the November 3 midterm elections, AP reported; Reuters said senators plan to bring it up for a vote in November. Sen. Moreno, who sponsors a bill to bar companies with more than 15 percent Chinese ownership from selling vehicles in the U.S., told CNBC it would not affect Mercedes-Benz.

heard_on_the_hill.headline: Wicker says U.S. must honor Taiwan commitments
heard_on_the_hill.body: Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker said U.S. security commitments to Taiwan must be upheld after meeting Taiwan's representative Alexander Yui, the Taipei Times reported. Four other Republican senators called on the administration to release more than $14 billion in stalled Taiwan security assistance. House Speaker Mike Johnson dismissed suggestions that the delayed package is being used as leverage in trade talks.

heard_on_the_hill.headline: Senators propose ban on Chinese optical modules
heard_on_the_hill.body: A bipartisan Senate group proposed banning Chinese-made optical modules from federal national-security systems, with a five-year grace period, Jiemian reported. ChiNext fell 4.53 percent on September 28 as the proposal weighed on sentiment, per Bloomberg. Reuters reported members of Congress are also moving to keep Chinese-origin datacenter hardware and software out of sensitive government systems.

heard_on_the_hill.headline: Lawmakers scrutinize F-35 parts sent to Hong Kong
heard_on_the_hill.body: F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong traveled a UPS route that regularly passes through China, Bloomberg reported, prompting U.S. lawmaker scrutiny. The Taipei Times said the Chinese government has taken possession of the stealth-coated components and not returned them.
heard_on_the_hill.event: F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong

heard_on_the_hill.headline: Republican chair seeks scrutiny of Seoul's China ties
heard_on_the_hill.body: A Republican committee chair called for greater scrutiny of South Korea's ties with China, Reuters reported, without detailing findings or proposed actions.
heard_on_the_hill.event: Scrutiny of South Korea's China ties

in_the_news.headline: Flyovers, pandas masked deep U.S.-China divides
in_the_news.body: Xi Jinping's September 23-25 state visit yielded tariff relief on $30 billion of goods each way, a two-month truce extension, a November AI dialogue and a Chinese pledge to buy U.S. coal, Reuters and the Financial Times reported. The New York Times said the flyovers and pandas masked deep divides on trade, AI and Taiwan. Trump said he will see Xi again in November.

in_the_news.headline: U.S. Taiwan policy unchanged after Xi's visit, Perdue says
in_the_news.body: A $14 billion Taiwan arms package remains stalled after the summit, AP reported, though Taiwan officials said Taipei is in "continuous talks" with Washington. Ambassador David Perdue said U.S. Taiwan policy has not shifted; Bloomberg noted Trump has not mentioned the package since the visit, saying only that Xi "knows how I feel."

in_the_news.headline: WSJ traces Houthi battlefield gains to arms supplied by Iran and China
in_the_news.body: U.S. intelligence assessments described to CNN say satellite imagery and intelligence support from Chinese groups helped Iran strike U.S. bases and threaten Hormuz shipping, a "dramatic improvement" in Iranian targeting. The Wall Street Journal traced Houthi gains in Yemen to weapons supplied by Iran and China. Ambassador David Perdue said Trump told Xi such assistance was "totally unacceptable" and received assurances.

in_the_news.headline: Philippines accuses China of obstructing resupply mission
in_the_news.body: The Philippines accused China of blocking a September 24 resupply mission to its grounded vessel at Second Thomas Shoal, the first such incident since 2024, Reuters and HKEJ reported. The U.S. embassy in Manila accused Beijing of "dangerous blocking and irresponsible manoeuvres," while China's coast guard said Manila "broke its promise." Joint PLA and coast guard drills followed at Scarborough Shoal on September 27.

in_the_news.event: U.S. assessment of Taiwan invasion timeline
in_the_news.headline: U.S. officials see Chinese invasion of Taiwan unlikely before 2028
in_the_news.body: Beijing is unlikely to use force against Taiwan before 2028, U.S. officials told Reuters, even though Xi has ordered the PLA to be ready by 2027. They cited an anti-corruption purge that leaves only two of seven Central Military Commission members in active service, and said Beijing may wait for Taiwan's 2028 election.

research_roundup.headline: The Limits of Trump and Xi’s Photo-Op Summit
research_roundup.body: CFR's David Sacks writes that Xi's visit "may have set a new high-water mark for symbolism and a new low for substance," with no consensus on major geopolitical issues, AI or a more sustainable economic relationship. The only clear winner, he argues, was Zoo Atlanta, though he says the meeting was not a complete failure.

research_roundup.headline: The Trump-Xi Summit Leaves Taiwan in Limbo
research_roundup.body: CNAS argues Xi used the summit to press Washington toward Beijing's position on Taiwan, but public accounts so far show no U.S. agreement to his request. Whether Trump can keep negotiating with Xi while making Taiwan harder to conquer "is now the measure of his cross-Strait policy."

research_roundup.headline: How do we deal with Chinese overcapacity?
research_roundup.body: Cecilia Malmström, Yeling Tan, Alicia García-Herrero and Nicolas Lamp note the summit reached no agreement on overcapacity and that an EU-China working group on "macroeconomic imbalances" formed in May has failed to produce results. They weigh whether managed trade or U.S.-EU coordination offers a way forward.

research_roundup.headline: Return of Tensions in the South China Sea Was a Matter of Time
research_roundup.body: Andrew Chubb of the Asia Society Policy Institute argues clashes between China and the Philippines were all but inevitable after two years of relative quiet. Confrontations have grown sharper and more frequent since July, he finds, from a July 20 fight near Second Thomas Shoal to a September 18 collision near Sabina Shoal.
